Covering the rare outcomes: stratified conformal prediction with size-optimal density scores for imbalanced regression

[Author 1]a,*, [Author 2]b

a [Affiliation 1, full postal address]; b [Affiliation 2, full postal address]

* Corresponding author: [e-mail address]

Abstract

Prediction intervals for regression are usually calibrated to hold on average over all outcomes, so they can systematically miss the rare, extreme outcomes that matter most in imbalanced regression. We study stratum-wise coverage, the probability that a prediction set contains the outcome given that the outcome lies in a target stratum such as the upper tail. Even the oracle interval with exact covariate-conditional coverage under-covers the tails: in a Gaussian model with half of the variance explained it covers 70.5% of the top decile. Calibrating conformal thresholds within target strata guarantees stratum-wise coverage for any score, so the score determines only efficiency. We show that conditional-density level sets with stratum-specific thresholds are the smallest stratum-valid sets, that their plug-in conformal version is asymptotically optimal, and that the gain over a normalised residual comes from reallocating coverage across inputs. The resulting method, stratified density-level conformal prediction (SDLC), was compared with 13 procedures on 31 OpenML-CTR23 datasets. At a nominal 90%, marginal and covariate-adaptive methods covered only 63.0%–78.3% of the outcomes in their worst-covered stratum, whereas stratified methods were consistent with exact validity. SDLC gave the smallest stratum-valid sets, smaller than bin-conditional conformal prediction on 24 of 31 datasets, and a pre-registered replication on 17 held-out datasets confirmed the ordering (size ratios between 0.841 and 0.984). Gains over a stratified normalised residual were small and came with lower coverage of the noisiest inputs. A decision study shows when dedicated conformal tail classifiers are preferable for alerts. Code and raw results are released.

Keywords: Conformal prediction; Imbalanced regression; Prediction intervals; Uncertainty quantification; Mondrian calibration; Extreme values; Distribution shift

1. Introduction

Many regression problems that intelligent systems are asked to solve are judged by how they handle the rare outcomes: the unusually expensive property, the exceptional salary, the extreme load on a power grid, the very toxic compound. These outcomes are rare by definition, so they are under-represented in training data, and models trained by minimising average loss shrink their predictions towards the bulk of the target distribution. This is the setting of imbalanced regression (Branco et al., 2017a; Ribeiro and Moniz, 2020; Yang et al., 2021), where a growing literature re-weights, re-samples or re-parameterises models so that point predictions for rare targets become more accurate.

Point predictions are only half of what a decision maker needs. Prediction sets (or intervals) with a coverage guarantee state how far the truth may be from the prediction, and conformal prediction delivers such guarantees in finite samples for any model, under exchangeability only (Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023; Lei et al., 2018; Vovk et al., 2005). Its standard guarantee, however, is marginal: the set contains the outcome with probability 1−α1-\alpha on average over all outcomes. When rare outcomes are what matter, the relevant question is different: when the outcome is extreme, how often does the set contain it? A marginal guarantee is silent on this question, because the frequent bulk of the distribution can be over-covered while the rare tails are under-covered and the average still equals 1−α1-\alpha.

A large body of work makes conformal sets adapt to the covariates, so that coverage holds approximately conditionally on XX (Chernozhukov et al., 2021; Gibbs et al., 2025; Izbicki et al., 2022; Romano et al., 2019). One might expect such sets also to protect rare outcomes. They do not, and better estimation would not change this: even the oracle set with exact coverage 1−α1-\alpha at every xx under-covers the tails of the target, because an extreme outcome typically combines a large signal with a large, unpredictable noise realisation that no XX-measurable set can anticipate. Coverage conditional on the target, which we call stratum-wise coverage, is a different property that must be targeted explicitly.

Calibrating conformal thresholds separately within bins of the observed outcome is the natural device for this purpose, and it is not new. Randahl et al. (2026) proposed it as bin-conditional conformal prediction (BCCP) for the heavily skewed distribution of conflict fatalities, and Wang et al. (2023) calibrate within bins of the outcome to obtain equal coverage across groups. Its finite-sample bin-wise validity is an instance of Mondrian (label-conditional) validity (Vovk, 2013; Vovk et al., 2005). Because the guarantee holds for any score, the open questions concern the score: which score makes stratum-valid sets smallest, where the gain comes from and what it costs. Two further questions are how the guarantee behaves when the target distribution shifts, and whether the answers hold beyond the data on which they were found. This paper makes four contributions.

  1. Theory of stratum-wise coverage. We quantify how far the oracle covariate-conditional set falls short in the tails: in a Gaussian model with half of the variance explained, it covers 70.5% of the top-decile outcomes (Proposition 1). Monte Carlo extensions to heavy-tailed signals and skewed noise show that the shortfall persists but that its shape depends on the model. For the oracle problem, conditional-density level sets with stratum-specific thresholds minimise expected size among all sets with stratum-wise coverage (Proposition 2), the per-stratum form of known level-set results (Kiyani et al., 2024; Lei et al., 2013; Sadinle et al., 2019). We prove that their plug-in conformal version is asymptotically size-optimal under uniform consistency of the density estimate (Proposition 3). We also show that, in a location–scale model, the gain over a normalised residual comes from reallocating coverage from high-noise to low-noise inputs, which explains both the efficiency and its cost. A corollary states when the known label-shift robustness of label-conditional calibration holds exactly for continuous outcomes and how it degrades otherwise.
  2. A method. Stratified density-level conformal prediction (SDLC) combines stratified calibration with a semiparametric location–scale density whose noise distribution is estimated nonparametrically from cross-fitted residuals. It has an exact, stratum-exact implementation whose cost is linear in the number of test points.
  3. A large benchmark with a confirmatory replication. On all 31 eligible OpenML-CTR23 datasets with 10 predefined splits, we compare 13 conformal procedures that share identical base models. They include BCCP, stratified versions of the normalised-residual, quantile and HPD scores, an ablation that isolates each component of the density score, and seven marginal or covariate-adaptive methods. The size comparisons are then replicated on 17 held-out datasets under an analysis plan that was made public before evaluation.
  4. Decision-oriented evidence. We evaluate tail alerts derived from prediction sets against dedicated conformal tail classifiers and conformal selection (Jin and Candès, 2023), with expected-cost curves for valuation problems, and we analyse robustness to target shift, imbalance-aware training, a second learner family, the miscoverage level, the strata and the calibration-set size.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 formalises the problem and analyses the oracle covariate-conditional set. Section 4 presents stratified calibration, its guarantees and the optimal score, and introduces SDLC. Section 5 describes the experimental design, Section 6 reports the results, Section 7 discusses implications and limitations, and Section 8 concludes.

2. Related work

Four lines of work meet in this paper: conformal regression with covariate-adaptive coverage, calibration within categories defined by the label, imbalanced regression, and conformal prediction under distribution shift.

2.1 Conformal regression and covariate-conditional coverage

Split (inductive) conformal prediction calibrates a nonconformity score of an arbitrary fitted regressor on held-out data and guarantees marginal coverage in finite samples under exchangeability (Lei et al., 2018; Papadopoulos et al., 2002; Vovk et al., 2005). Much subsequent work changes the score so that the sets adapt to the covariates. Locally weighted (normalised) conformal prediction divides absolute residuals by an estimate of their spread (Lei et al., 2018); conformalised quantile regression (CQR) calibrates the interval between two estimated conditional quantiles (Romano et al., 2019; Sesia and Candès, 2020); and distributional conformal prediction (DCP) uses the probability integral transform of an estimated conditional distribution function (Chernozhukov et al., 2021). Conformal predictive distributions (Vovk et al., 2019) and jackknife+/CV+ intervals, which reuse all data at higher computational cost (Barber et al., 2021a), are further alternatives. A family of methods builds sets from density estimates: density level sets, conformalised without covariates and asymptotically optimal (Lei et al., 2013) and extended to regression by local conformal bands (Lei and Wasserman, 2014); Dist-split and CD-split (Izbicki et al., 2020); HPD-split, which conformalises highest-density regions of an estimated conditional density (Izbicki et al., 2022); conformal sets from conditional histograms, which adapt to skewness (Sesia and Romano, 2021); regression-as-classification, which learns a density over a discretised target (Guha et al., 2024); and conformal thresholded intervals, which threshold the estimated conditional quantiles to shorten the sets (Luo and Zhou, 2025). Under coverage constraints indexed by a finite-dimensional class of covariate shifts, length-optimal sets are level sets of the conditional density with a covariate-dependent level (Kiyani et al., 2024). SDLC uses a score from this family but calibrates it with stratum-specific thresholds.

These methods target approximate covariate-conditional coverage, P{Y∈C(X)|X=x}≈1−αP\{Y\in C(X)\,|\, X=x\}\approx 1-\alpha, which cannot be guaranteed in finite samples without further assumptions (Barber et al., 2021b). The literature has therefore pursued relaxed guarantees and approximations: local conformal bands with asymptotic conditional validity (Lei and Wasserman, 2014); conditional calibration, which guarantees coverage over a user-specified class of covariate groups or shifts (Gibbs et al., 2025); localised calibration, which weights calibration points by their proximity to the test point in covariate space (Guan, 2023; Hore and Barber, 2025); calibration within the cells of covariate partitions learned by regression trees (Cabezas et al., 2025) or by the leaf paths of gradient-boosted trees (Santos et al., 2026); and learned scores or adjusted regressors that reduce conditional miscoverage (Gao et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024). In applied expert systems, conformal prediction serves as an uncertainty layer, for example for option prices (Bastos, 2024), tropical-cyclone track forecasts (Meng and Song, 2024) and the carbonation depth of recycled-aggregate concrete (Hajibabaee et al., 2025). All of these approaches are marginal or condition, exactly or approximately, on functions of XX, and Proposition 1 (Section 3) shows that, in a Gaussian model, even exact covariate-conditional coverage leaves extreme outcomes under-covered. Covariate-adaptive scores are therefore complementary to stratified calibration rather than a substitute for it.

2.2 Category-, label- and bin-conditional calibration

Mondrian conformal predictors (Vovk et al., 2022, 2005) assign each example to a category through a taxonomy that may depend on both the object and its label, and calibrate separately within each category; this yields finite-sample coverage conditional on the category (Angelopoulos et al., 2024). Vovk (2013) distinguished object-, label- and training-conditional validity and showed that Mondrian inductive conformal predictors achieve category-conditional, and in particular label-conditional, validity; Toccaceli and Gammerman (2019) studied label-conditional inductive Mondrian predictors and their combination.

In classification, the corresponding property is class-conditional coverage. When classes are many and calibration examples per class are few, clustered conformal prediction pools classes with similar score distributions (Ding et al., 2023), a device analogous to merging sparse target strata; BCOPS constructs label-conditional sets from density estimates (Guan and Tibshirani, 2022); and Mondrian conformal prediction has been applied in this journal to product verification (Oucheikh et al., 2022). Closest to our optimality result is work on set-valued classifiers with class-specific error control (Lei, 2014), in particular Sadinle et al. (2019), who showed that the least ambiguous classifier under class-specific coverage thresholds the conditional class probabilities p(y|x)p(y\,|\, x) with class-specific cut-offs. Proposition 2 is the same characterisation for a continuous outcome, with Lebesgue measure as the size and target strata in place of classes. Group-conditional coverage is also the basis of equalized coverage across protected groups in fair prediction (Romano et al., 2020). Kandinsky conformal prediction (Bairaktari et al., 2025) provides conditional coverage for overlapping or fractional groups defined jointly on covariates and labels, includes regression, and contains covariate-group-conditional, class-conditional and Mondrian conformal prediction as special cases, with a high-probability guarantee whose slack grows with the complexity of the group class. Disjoint target strata are its simplest label-defined groups, for which Mondrian calibration gives an exact finite-sample guarantee; overlapping groups (for example strata and deciles together) and weighted groups (for example tilts of the target distribution) are a natural way to refine the guarantee beyond a single partition.

In regression, Mondrian categories have mostly been defined through the covariates or the fitted model: by binning difficulty estimates (Boström and Johansson, 2020), with interpretable regression trees (Johansson et al., 2018), by clusters of the covariates (Sousa et al., 2024) and by quartiles of out-of-fold point predictions (Boruah, 2026a); Mondrian taxonomies have also been applied to conformal predictive distributions (Boström et al., 2021). The last study reports that split conformal intervals for steel fatigue strength, although marginally valid, under-cover the highest-strength quartile; a follow-up shows that worst-bin coverage statistics are biased downwards and proposes a null correction (Boruah, 2026b). Because the categories are functions of XX, the resulting guarantees do not extend to coverage conditional on YY.

We are aware of two regression methods that calibrate within bins of the outcome itself. Wang et al. (2023) define equal opportunity of coverage, which requires coverage to be equal across groups of a sensitive attribute conditionally on the true outcome; their binned fair quantile regression (BFQR) splits YY into equal-mass bins and calibrates within each combination of group and bin, with a conformal step that maintains coverage, and they illustrate that standard methods mis-cover the head and tail bins of the outcome. Their aim is fairness, but the binning device is the same. Their binned fair quantile regression (BFQR) forms equal-mass bins of the calibration outcomes, takes within each group and bin the βm\beta_m-quantile of conformalised quantile-regression scores, and chooses the bin levels βm\beta_m to minimise the average width subject to ∑mβm/M=1−α\sum_m\beta_m/M=1-\alpha; their Theorem 4.1 shows that coverage in each group and bin lies between βm\beta_m and βm+1/(na,m+1)\beta_m+1/(n_{a,m}+1). Coverage is thus equalised across groups within a bin but deliberately traded across bins. The most closely related work is the bin-conditional conformal prediction (BCCP) of Randahl et al. (2026), motivated by the heavily skewed distribution of fatalities from armed conflict. BCCP partitions the calibration scores by user-defined bins of the observed outcome, runs split conformal prediction with a residual score within each bin over a grid of candidate outcomes, and returns either the union of the per-bin sets, which may be discontiguous, or its hull (“contiguized” sets). The authors state that BCCP guarantees coverage within each bin under within-bin exchangeability, describe it as a hybrid of label-conditional (Mondrian) and split conformal prediction, and evaluate it on simulations and on conflict fatalities.

The stratified calibration step of the present paper (Section 4, Eqs. 3–4) coincides with BCCP: with the absolute-residual score and the strata as bins it is BCCP, and taking the convex hull, as in our hull variant, gives its contiguized form. Its finite-sample validity (Theorem 1) is an instance of Mondrian validity and is not claimed as new; Randahl et al. (2026) note that it holds for any score. BCCP leaves open which score yields the smallest bin-valid sets, how the score’s efficiency comes about, and how the guarantee behaves under label shift. The present paper addresses these questions: the oracle analysis of covariate-conditional sets (Proposition 1), the size-optimal score under per-stratum coverage and the asymptotic optimality of its plug-in version (Propositions 2 and 3), the SDLC procedure built on them, the label-shift analysis (Corollary 1), and large-scale evidence in which BCCP, stratified versions of the normalised-residual, quantile and HPD scores, and marginal and covariate-adaptive methods serve as baselines.

2.3 Imbalanced regression and its uncertainty

Imbalanced regression concerns problems in which the target values that matter most are rare in the training data (Branco et al., 2017a; Ribeiro and Moniz, 2020). Utility-based regression encodes the non-uniform importance of targets through relevance and utility functions (Torgo and Ribeiro, 2007), and precision and recall for regression (Torgo and Ribeiro, 2009) and the SERA metric (Ribeiro and Moniz, 2020) evaluate point predictions on the relevant, typically extreme, part of the target range. Data-level methods re-balance the training set: SMOTER (Torgo et al., 2013) and SMOGN, which adds Gaussian noise (Branco et al., 2017b), synthesise examples with rare targets, and Avelino et al. (2024) survey and benchmark such re-sampling strategies. Recent contributions in this journal include oversampling with nearest neighbours and autoencoders (Belhaouari et al., 2024), the refinement of oversampled examples by a generative adversarial network (Alahyari and Domaratzki, 2026), a hybrid of data-level and algorithm-level balancing (Shahbazi et al., 2026) and soft-computing techniques that actively address imbalance (Arteaga et al., 2023). Algorithm-level methods re-weight the loss: DenseWeight weights training examples inversely to the estimated density of their target (Steininger et al., 2021), label and feature distribution smoothing exploit the similarity of nearby targets in deep models (Yang et al., 2021), and Balanced MSE corrects the regression loss for the imbalance of the training label distribution (Ren et al., 2022).

Uncertainty has entered this literature mainly as a means to better point predictions or as a by-product of probabilistic modelling. Variational imbalanced regression obtains uncertainty estimates through probabilistic smoothing (Wang and Wang, 2023), and UQDIR identifies rare samples through epistemic uncertainty and re-samples them with a weight function to improve accuracy (Dolar et al., 2025); neither provides a coverage guarantee. Extreme conformal prediction addresses a different difficulty, very high confidence levels, by combining extreme-value theory with conformal prediction (Pasche et al., 2026). Guarantees on how often prediction sets contain the rare targets themselves, the uncertainty counterpart of the relevance-based evaluation above, have so far come from conflict forecasting and fair regression (Randahl et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2023) rather than from the imbalanced-regression literature (Section 2.2). Where the decision is only whether a unit’s outcome is extreme, dedicated procedures exist: conformal selection flags units whose outcome exceeds a threshold with control of the false discovery rate (Jin and Candès, 2023), and a class-conditional conformal classifier on the event “outcome in the tail” controls the miss rate. We use both as baselines for tail alerts (Section 6).

2.4 Distribution shift

Weighted conformal prediction restores validity under covariate shift by re-weighting calibration scores with the likelihood ratio of the covariate distributions (Tibshirani et al., 2019). Under label shift, also called target shift, the marginal distribution of YY changes while the conditional distribution of XX given YY does not. For classification, Podkopaev and Ramdas (2021) study conformal prediction under label shift, using re-weighted and label-conditional calibration. For regression, Yi et al. (2025) identify the likelihood ratio under target shift and construct highest-density sets from a weight-adjusted conditional density, and Lee et al. (2026) combine a label-shift-adjusted Bayesian score with importance weighting. The re-weighting approaches estimate the shift (Lee et al., 2026; Yi et al., 2025); label-conditional calibration in classification needs no estimate, because a label shift re-weights whole classes (Podkopaev and Ramdas, 2021).

Stratified calibration carries this property over to regression: it needs no estimate of the shift, because a guarantee that holds within every stratum is unaffected by changes in the stratum probabilities. This invariance is exact when the shift re-weights whole strata, that is, when the conditional distribution of (X,Y)(X,Y) within each stratum is unchanged (Corollary 1). If the density ratio varies inside a stratum, the within-stratum distribution changes and the guarantee holds only approximately, which our experiments quantify under target tilting (Section 5).

Positioning of this work. Calibration within outcome strata (Randahl et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2023) and its per-stratum validity (Randahl et al., 2026; Vovk, 2013; Vovk et al., 2005) are established, and the present paper takes them as given. It asks instead why such calibration is needed even when covariate-conditional coverage is exact (Proposition 1), which score makes stratum-valid sets smallest and where the gain comes from (Propositions 2 and 3, SDLC), and when the guarantee survives label shift (Corollary 1). It then examines these questions empirically on 31 OpenML-CTR23 datasets (Fischer et al., 2023) with 10 repetitions each, under a protocol fixed in advance, against BCCP, stratified normalised-residual, quantile and HPD scores and marginal and covariate-adaptive conformal methods, and replicates the main comparisons on 17 held-out datasets under a pre-registered analysis plan. For imbalanced regression, this complements methods that improve accuracy on rare targets with a guarantee on how often prediction sets contain them.

3. Problem formulation

3.1 Target-conditional coverage

Let (X,Y)∈𝒳×ℝ(X,Y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathbb{R} have joint law PP, with marginal law PXP_X of the covariates. A prediction set is a map CC from 𝒳\mathcal{X} to subsets of ℝ\mathbb{R} whose graph {(x,y):y∈C(x)}\{(x,y):y\in C(x)\} is jointly measurable. Split conformal prediction (Lei et al., 2018; Papadopoulos et al., 2002) guarantees marginal coverage P{Y∈C(X)}≥1−αP\{Y\in C(X)\}\ge 1-\alpha, and much recent work targets approximate covariate-conditional coverage P{Y∈C(X)|X=x}≈1−αP\{Y\in C(X)\,|\, X=x\}\approx 1-\alpha (Gibbs et al., 2025; Izbicki et al., 2022; Romano et al., 2019), which cannot be guaranteed in finite samples without further assumptions (Barber et al., 2021b).

In imbalanced regression the outcomes of interest are rare target values. Let e1<…<eK−1e_1<\dots<e_{K-1} be cut points and B1=(−∞,e1)B_1=(-\infty,e_1), Bk=[ek−1,ek)B_k=[e_{k-1},e_k) for 1<k<K1<k<K, BK=[eK−1,∞)B_K=[e_{K-1},\infty) the resulting target strata, for instance the lower tail, the bulk and the upper tail, with pk=P(Y∈Bk)>0p_k=P(Y\in B_k)>0. We call Covk(C)=P{Y∈C(X)|Y∈Bk},k=1,…,K,(1)\operatorname{Cov}_k(C)=P\{Y\in C(X)\,|\, Y\in B_k\},\qquad k=1,\ldots,K, \qquad (1) the stratum-wise (target-conditional) coverage of CC. It answers the question that matters when extremes are costly: when the outcome is extreme, how often does the prediction set contain it? It is the regression analogue of class-conditional coverage in classification (Sadinle et al., 2019; Vovk, 2013; Vovk et al., 2005) and the outcome-conditional notion behind equal opportunity of coverage (Wang et al., 2023) and bin-conditional conformal prediction (Randahl et al., 2026). Integrating (2) over strata of YY (Table 1): for a predictor that explains half of the variance, the oracle covariate-conditional interval covers 70.5% of the top-10% outcomes and 37.5% of the top-1% outcomes, against 94.9% of the central 80%; with R2=0.9R^2=0.9 it covers 86.2% of the top decile. Proposition 1 is specific to the Gaussian model, and the shape of the coverage profile is not universal. Table 1 therefore also reports Monte Carlo values for heavy-tailed signals and for skewed noise (oracle XX-conditional shortest sets; details in the table note). With a Student-tt signal and Gaussian noise the tail strata are still under-covered at R2=0.5R^2=0.5 (top 10%: 0.648 for t3t_3), but coverage no longer vanishes in the extreme tail: for t3t_3 the top 1% is covered at 0.625, because extreme outcomes are then mostly produced by extreme signals, which a covariate-conditional set follows. With right-skewed Gamma noise the oracle over-covers the lower decile (0.987) and covers only 0.418 of the top decile and 0.029 of the top 1%. In every case at least one tail stratum is covered well below 1−α1-\alpha. Tail under-coverage of standard conformal sets has been reported empirically (Boruah, 2026a; Randahl et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2023); Proposition 1 and its extensions show that it persists for the oracle, so better covariate adaptivity cannot remove it. To guarantee coverage in rare strata, a set must be calibrated against the distribution of (X,Y)(X,Y) given Y∈BkY\in B_k, which is what stratified calibration does.

4. Stratified calibration and the optimal score

4.1 Stratified (Mondrian) calibration

Data are split into a proper training set 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} and a calibration set 𝒟cal={(Xi,Yi)}i=1n\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}=\{(X_i,Y_i)\}_{i=1}^n. Using 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} only, we fit a nonconformity score s:𝒳×ℝ→ℝ∪{+∞}s:\mathcal{X}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} (small values = conforming) and choose the cut points, e.g. at quantiles of the training targets. Let k(y)k(y) be the stratum containing yy, Ik={i:Yi∈Bk}I_k=\{i:Y_i\in B_k\}, nk=|Ik|n_k=|I_k|, and, for levels αk∈(0,1)\alpha_k\in(0,1), q̂k=the rk-th smallest value of {s(Xi,Yi):i∈Ik},rk=⌈(nk+1)(1−αk)⌉,(3)\hat q_k=\text{the }r_k\text{-th smallest value of }\{s(X_i,Y_i):i\in I_k\},\qquad r_k=\lceil (n_k+1)(1-\alpha_k)\rceil, \qquad (3) with q̂k=+∞\hat q_k=+\infty if rk>nkr_k>n_k, which happens exactly when nk<1/αk−1n_k<1/\alpha_k-1 (i.e. nk≤8n_k\le 8 for αk=0.1\alpha_k=0.1). The stratified prediction set is Ĉ(x)={y∈ℝ:s(x,y)≤q̂k(y)}=⋃k=1K{y∈Bk:s(x,y)≤q̂k}.(4)\hat C(x)=\{y\in\mathbb{R}: s(x,y)\le \hat q_{k(y)}\}=\bigcup_{k=1}^K\{y\in B_k: s(x,y)\le\hat q_k\}. \qquad (4) The threshold applied to a candidate value yy is that of the stratum of that candidate, not of a prediction; this is what makes the guarantee target-conditional. Equation (4) is an inductive Mondrian conformal predictor whose taxonomy assigns each example to the stratum of its label (Toccaceli and Gammerman, 2019; Vovk, 2013; Vovk et al., 2005), and it is not new for regression. With the absolute-residual score it is the bin-conditional conformal prediction (BCCP) of Randahl et al. (2026), who report either the union (4) or its convex hull and note that the bin-wise guarantee holds for any score. Wang et al. (2023) calibrate quantile-regression scores within equal-mass bins of YY and groups of a sensitive attribute, at bin-specific levels that are optimised for width and average to 1−α1-\alpha, and prove the corresponding group-and-bin-conditional guarantee. Kandinsky conformal prediction (Bairaktari et al., 2025) covers far richer families: overlapping or fractional groups defined jointly on covariates and labels, with a high-probability guarantee whose slack grows with the dimension of the group class. Disjoint target strata are its simplest special case, for which (4) gives the exact finite-sample guarantee below. When every sub-level set {y:s(x,y)≤q}\{y:s(x,y)\le q\} is an interval, as for residual or quantile scores, Ĉ(x)\hat C(x) is a union of at most KK intervals; density scores with a multimodal estimate can produce more pieces.

The following guarantee is the standard label-conditional Mondrian property (Vovk, 2013; Vovk et al., 2005); for bins of a continuous outcome it is stated by Wang et al. (2023, Thm. 4.1) and Randahl et al. (2026). We restate it for an arbitrary score, with the edge cases used later, and give the proof in Appendix A for completeness.

Theorem 1 (stratum-wise validity of Mondrian calibration). Suppose that, conditionally on 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}, the points (X1,Y1),…,(Xn,Yn),(Xn+1,Yn+1)(X_1,Y_1),\ldots,(X_n,Y_n),(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1}) are exchangeable, and let pk=P(Yn+1∈Bk|𝒟tr)p_k=P(Y_{n+1}\in B_k\,|\,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}). Then for every kk with pk>0p_k>0, P{Yn+1∈Ĉ(Xn+1)|Yn+1∈Bk,𝒟tr}≥1−αk,(5)P\{Y_{n+1}\in\hat C(X_{n+1})\,|\, Y_{n+1}\in B_k,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}\}\ \ge\ 1-\alpha_k, \qquad (5) and consequently P{Yn+1∈Ĉ(Xn+1)|𝒟tr}≥1−∑kpkαk≥1−maxkαkP\{Y_{n+1}\in\hat C(X_{n+1})\,|\,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}\}\ge 1-\sum_kp_k\alpha_k\ge 1-\max_k\alpha_k. If the scores within stratum kk are almost surely distinct and finite, then also P{Yn+1∈Ĉ(Xn+1)|Yn+1∈Bk,nk,𝒟tr}≤1−αk+1/(nk+1)P\{Y_{n+1}\in\hat C(X_{n+1})\,|\, Y_{n+1}\in B_k,n_k,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}\}\le 1-\alpha_k+1/(n_k+1). The levels αk\alpha_k may depend on nkn_k, and the score and strata may be any functions of 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}.

The guarantee holds for any score. A consequence concerns shifts of the target distribution between calibration and deployment; it collects known facts, specialised to target strata.

Corollary 1 (target shift). Let 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}} be i.i.d. from PP and let the test point be drawn from QQ, independently of 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}} and 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}. Write Pk=P(⋅|Y∈Bk)P_k=P(\cdot\,|\, Y\in B_k) and Qk=Q(⋅|Y∈Bk)Q_k=Q(\cdot\,|\, Y\in B_k) for the within-stratum laws of the pair (X,Y)(X,Y) and πk=Q(Y∈Bk)\pi_k=Q(Y\in B_k); assume pk>0p_k>0 whenever πk>0\pi_k>0. (i) If Qk=PkQ_k=P_k for every kk with πk>0\pi_k>0 (the shift re-weights whole strata), then Q{Y∈Ĉ(X)|Y∈Bk}≥1−αkQ\{Y\in\hat C(X)\,|\, Y\in B_k\}\ge 1-\alpha_k for every such kk, and Q{Y∈Ĉ(X)}≥1−∑kπkαkQ\{Y\in\hat C(X)\}\ge 1-\sum_k\pi_k\alpha_k whatever the πk\pi_k. (ii) For an arbitrary shift, Q{Y∈Ĉ(X)|Y∈Bk}≥1−αk−dTV(Qk,Pk)Q\{Y\in\hat C(X)\,|\, Y\in B_k\}\ge 1-\alpha_k-d_{\operatorname{TV}}(Q_k,P_k). (iii) Under label shift, Q(⋅|Y=y)=P(⋅|Y=y)Q(\cdot\,|\, Y=y)=P(\cdot\,|\, Y=y) with density ratio w=dQY/dPYw=dQ_Y/dP_Y; let mkm_k and MkM_k be the essential infimum and supremum of ww on BkB_k, 0<mk≤Mk<∞0<m_k\le M_k<\infty. Then Q{Y∉Ĉ(X)|Y∈Bk}≤(Mk/mk)αkQ\{Y\notin\hat C(X)\,|\, Y\in B_k\}\le(M_k/m_k)\,\alpha_k and dTV(Qk,Pk)≤tanh{log(Mk/mk)/4}d_{\operatorname{TV}}(Q_k,P_k)\le\tanh\{\log(M_k/m_k)/4\}.

The proof is in Appendix A. Part (i) is the continuous-outcome form of the label-shift robustness of label-conditional coverage in classification (Angelopoulos et al., 2024; Podkopaev and Ramdas, 2021). The point specific to a continuous outcome is that a label shift generally also changes the distribution of YY within a stratum; exactness then requires that the joint law of (X,Y)(X,Y) inside each stratum be unchanged, and a stable covariate distribution alone is not sufficient. Part (ii) is the total-variation form of the coverage-gap bounds of Barber et al. (2023, sec. 4.5), applied within a stratum, and part (iii) is the standard consequence of a bounded likelihood ratio. Both bounds are loose for the shifts studied in Experiment 4, whose density ratios are unbounded on the open tail strata, so they explain the direction of the effect rather than its size: degradation is small when the density ratio varies little across each stratum, which favours narrow strata at the price of fewer calibration points per stratum. Marginally calibrated sets enjoy no analogue of (i): their coverage under QQ is ∑kπkCovk\sum_k\pi_k\operatorname{Cov}_k, which can be as low as minkCovk\min_k\operatorname{Cov}_k. Unlike re-weighting approaches (Lee et al., 2026; Podkopaev and Ramdas, 2021; Yi et al., 2025; for covariate shift Tibshirani et al., 2019), stratified calibration needs no estimate of the shift, but it is exact only for shifts that act on the stratum probabilities.

4.2 The smallest sets with stratum-wise coverage

Theorem 1 leaves the score free, so validity is never the issue; the score determines how large the sets are. For a prediction set CC let |C(x)||C(x)| be its Lebesgue measure and 𝔼|C(X)|=∫|C(x)|PX(dx)\mathbb{E}|C(X)|=\int|C(x)|\,P_X(dx) its expected size. The size-optimal sets are density level sets, by the Neyman–Pearson argument that underlies conformal density level sets (Lei et al., 2013), least-ambiguous set-valued classifiers with class-specific coverage (Lei, 2014; Sadinle et al., 2019) and, for coverage constraints indexed by groups or shifts of the covariates, the length-optimal sets of Kiyani et al. (2024), whose level depends on xx. The constraints in (1) are indexed by the label instead, so the problem separates by stratum and the solution has thresholds that are constant within each stratum. We state the result for this case because it identifies the score that stratified calibration should use.

Proposition 2 (size-optimal stratum-wise sets). Suppose the conditional law of YY given XX has a Lebesgue density f(y|x)f(y\,|\, x), that f(Y|X)>0f(Y\,|\, X)>0 almost surely, and that for each kk the random variable f(Y|X)f(Y\,|\, X) has a continuous distribution conditionally on Y∈BkY\in B_k. Fix α1,…,αK∈(0,1)\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_K\in(0,1). Then there are thresholds tk>0t_k>0 with P{f(Y|X)≥tk|Y∈Bk}=1−αkP\{f(Y\,|\, X)\ge t_k\,|\, Y\in B_k\}=1-\alpha_k, and the set C⋆(x)=⋃k=1K{y∈Bk:f(y|x)≥tk}(6)C^\star(x)=\bigcup_{k=1}^K\{y\in B_k: f(y\,|\, x)\ge t_k\} \qquad (6) satisfies Covk(C⋆)=1−αk\operatorname{Cov}_k(C^\star)=1-\alpha_k for all kk. Every prediction set CC with Covk(C)≥1−αk\operatorname{Cov}_k(C)\ge 1-\alpha_k for all kk satisfies 𝔼|C(X)∩Bk|≥𝔼|C⋆(X)∩Bk|\mathbb{E}|C(X)\cap B_k|\ge\mathbb{E}|C^\star(X)\cap B_k| for every kk, and hence 𝔼|C(X)|≥𝔼|C⋆(X)|\mathbb{E}|C(X)|\ge\mathbb{E}|C^\star(X)|.

The proof (Appendix A) is the per-stratum Neyman–Pearson argument. Since the inequality holds for every realisation of a set built from data independent of the test point, C⋆C^\star also minimises expected size among data-dependent (e.g. conformal) sets whose stratum-wise coverage, averaged over the data, is at least 1−αk1-\alpha_k. With K=1K=1 it reduces to a single-threshold conditional-density level set; HPD-split (Izbicki et al., 2022) instead uses an xx-specific threshold, whose oracle is the highest-density region of each conditional distribution. Proposition 2 is an oracle statement. The next result shows that stratified calibration of a consistent density estimate attains it asymptotically (strata estimated from training quantiles converge to fixed cut points, which we take as given); its proof (Appendix A) follows the plug-in arguments of Lei et al. (2013) and Izbicki et al. (2022).

Proposition 3 (asymptotic size-optimality of the plug-in procedure). Let the assumptions of Proposition 2 hold, and suppose in addition that the distribution function of f(Y|X)f(Y\,|\, X) given Y∈BkY\in B_k is strictly increasing at tkt_k for every kk. Let f̂\hat f be estimated from 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} of size NN, let εN=supx,y|f̂(y|x)−f(y|x)|→0\varepsilon_N=\sup_{x,y}|\hat f(y\,|\, x)-f(y\,|\, x)|\to0 in probability, and let Ĉ\hat C be the stratified set (3)–(4) with score s=−f̂s=-\hat f, fixed strata B1,…,BKB_1,\ldots,B_K and n→∞n\to\infty calibration points. Then −q̂k→tk-\hat q_k\to t_k in probability for every kk, and 𝔼X|Ĉ(X)△C⋆(X)|→0in probability,(7)\mathbb{E}_X\big|\hat C(X)\,\triangle\,C^\star(X)\big|\ \to\ 0\quad\text{in probability,} \qquad (7) where 𝔼X\mathbb{E}_X averages over a new X∼PXX\sim P_X given the data. In particular 𝔼X|Ĉ(X)|→𝔼|C⋆(X)|\mathbb{E}_X|\hat C(X)|\to\mathbb{E}|C^\star(X)| while (5) holds for every nn.

Four consequences guide the method.

The optimal score. The size-optimal score is the conditional density, s(x,y)=−f(y|x)s(x,y)=-f(y\,|\, x), combined with stratum-specific thresholds; a single threshold is optimal only for marginal coverage.

The price of stratum-wise validity. Every set that satisfies the stratum constraints has marginal coverage at least 1−α‾1-\bar\alpha, α‾=∑kpkαk\bar\alpha=\sum_kp_k\alpha_k. Hence 𝔼|C⋆(X)|\mathbb{E}|C^\star(X)| is at least the expected size of the size-optimal marginal set at level 1−α‾1-\bar\alpha, a single-threshold density level set; under the assumptions of Proposition 2 the two coincide if and only if t1=…=tKt_1=\dots=t_K, i.e. if and only if that marginal set already has coverage 1−αk1-\alpha_k in every stratum. With a common level αk=α\alpha_k=\alpha this difference is the price, in size, of stratum-wise validity.

Coverage is reallocated across inputs. In a location–scale model f(y|x)=g{(y−μ(x))/σ(x)}/σ(x)f(y\,|\, x)=g\{(y-\mu(x))/\sigma(x)\}/\sigma(x) the optimal set is, in standardised units u=(y−μ(x))/σ(x)u=(y-\mu(x))/\sigma(x), {u:g(u)≥tkσ(x)}\{u: g(u)\ge t_k\sigma(x)\} within stratum kk. Its standardised width therefore shrinks as σ(x)\sigma(x) grows, and it is empty whenever tkσ(x)>maxgt_k\sigma(x)>\max g: the oracle spends coverage on inputs where it is cheap and withholds it where it is expensive. The stratified normalised residual (S-NCP), whose standardised width does not depend on xx, is optimal only when σ\sigma is constant. The size advantage of the density score over S-NCP thus comes partly from the factor 1/σ(x)1/\sigma(x) and is paid for by lower coverage, and occasionally empty sets, for the noisiest inputs. Stratum-wise coverage is unaffected, but covariate-conditional coverage across levels of σ(x)\sigma(x) is not equalised (Section 6 reports both). Users who need comparable coverage across noise levels should prefer S-NCP.

Shape. C⋆(x)C^\star(x) need not be an interval even when f(⋅|x)f(\cdot\,|\, x) is unimodal: thresholds differ across strata (typically tkt_k is smaller in a rare tail stratum), so C⋆(x)C^\star(x) can contain a piece of a tail stratum while excluding part of an adjacent stratum.

Scope. The optimality refers to size averaged over the covariate law PXP_X of the calibration population; under a shifted QQ, C⋆C^\star remains valid in the sense of Corollary 1(i) but is no longer size-optimal. For targets with atoms (ties, zero inflation) Theorem 1 is unaffected, whereas Lebesgue size is degenerate at an atom and the size-optimal set contains every atom; on such data a smooth density score is valid but not size-optimal.

4.3 The proposed method: stratified density-level conformal prediction (SDLC)

SDLC instantiates (3)–(4) with the plug-in score s(x,y)=−f̂(y|x)s(x,y)=-\hat f(y\,|\, x), where f̂\hat f is estimated on 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}. By Theorem 1 the guarantee (5) holds for any f̂\hat f; Propositions 2 and 3 motivate the score. We use the semiparametric location–scale estimator f̂(y|x)=1σ̂(x)ĝ(y−μ̂(x)σ̂(x)).(8)\hat f(y\,|\, x)=\frac{1}{\hat\sigma(x)}\,\hat g\!\left(\frac{y-\hat\mu(x)}{\hat\sigma(x)}\right). \qquad (8) Here μ̂\hat\mu is a gradient-boosted regression of YY on XX, and σ̂(x)=max{σ̃(x),𝜍}\hat\sigma(x)=\max\{\tilde\sigma(x),\varsigma\}, where σ̃\tilde\sigma is a gradient-boosted regression of the absolute out-of-fold residuals |Y−μ̂−j(X)||Y-\hat\mu_{-j}(X)| (three folds), the spread estimate of locally weighted conformal prediction (Lei et al., 2018). The floor 𝜍=max{10−3sd(Ytr),0.05median|Y−μ̂−j(X)|}\varsigma=\max\{10^{-3}\operatorname{sd}(Y_{\mathrm{tr}}),\,0.05\,\mathrm{median}|Y-\hat\mu_{-j}(X)|\} is shared by every method that uses σ̂\hat\sigma. The noise density is a defensive mixture ĝ=(1−ϵ)ĝKDE+ϵt2(⋅/ŝ)/ŝ,ϵ=0.01,(9)\hat g=(1-\epsilon)\,\hat g_{\mathrm{KDE}}+\epsilon\,t_2(\cdot/\hat s)/\hat s,\qquad \epsilon=0.01, \qquad (9) of a Gaussian kernel density estimate (Silverman bandwidth) and a Student-t2t_2 density with robust scale ŝ=IQR/1.349\hat s=\mathrm{IQR}/1.349. The mixture is fitted to cross-fitted standardised residuals: the out-of-fold residuals of fold jj are divided by a scale model trained on the other two folds, so that neither μ̂\hat\mu nor σ̂\hat\sigma has seen the residual it standardises. (Standardising by an in-sample scale fit shrinks the residuals, in our data by a median factor of 1.14 in standard deviation, and makes ĝ\hat g too narrow.) The defensive component gives ĝ\hat g polynomial tails, so that targets far outside the training residuals still receive a smooth, strictly decreasing density rather than an arbitrary floor. The noise density is nonparametric, so (8) captures skewness and heavy tails of the error distribution, and heteroscedasticity enters through σ̂\hat\sigma. If Y=μ(X)+σ(X)εY=\mu(X)+\sigma(X)\varepsilon with ε\varepsilon independent of XX, (8) can be consistent, so Proposition 3 applies. Otherwise SDLC targets the optimal sets of the best location–scale approximation, which affects size but never validity.

Three alternatives are evaluated as ablations. SDLC-N replaces ĝ\hat g by the standard normal density (with the same defensive component), so that its score differs from the normalised residual only through the factor 1/σ̂(x)1/\hat\sigma(x). An exploratory two-piece variant replaces σ̂\hat\sigma by side-specific scales σ̂−(x)\hat\sigma_-(x) below μ̂(x)\hat\mu(x) and σ̂+(x)\hat\sigma_+(x) above it. A fully nonparametric histogram density is obtained from a multiclass gradient-boosted classifier over 40 equal-mass target bins (a “regression-as-classification” density, cf. Sesia and Romano (2021) and Guha et al. (2024)).

4.4 Implementation

Strata. The primary stratification uses the training-target quantiles 0.10,0.25,0.75,0.900.10, 0.25, 0.75, 0.90 (K=5K=5: lower tail, lower shoulder, bulk, upper shoulder, upper tail). With tied targets coinciding cut points are merged and empty strata removed, so the realised number of strata and their masses can differ from the nominal values; realised values are reported per dataset, and the sensitivity analyses repeat the main comparisons on the datasets whose realised tail strata are close to nominal.

Exact scores and the domain. Calibration scores are computed exactly at the observed target, Si=−f̂(Yi|Xi)S_i=-\hat f(Y_i\,|\, X_i). Sets are restricted to a bounded domain D=[miny−0.05r,maxy+0.05r]D=[\min y-0.05r,\max y+0.05r] of the training targets (rr the training range), intersected with [0,∞)[0,\infty) when all training targets are non-negative. A point with Y∉DY\notin D receives the score +∞+\infty, stays in its stratum, and counts as not covered. Membership of a test target is decided by the same exact rule, Yn+1∈Ĉ(Xn+1)Y_{n+1}\in\hat C(X_{n+1}) iff s(Xn+1,Yn+1)≤q̂k(Yn+1)s(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1})\le\hat q_{k(Y_{n+1})}, so the lower bound of Theorem 1 applies to the reported coverage. Two details follow from the domain. First, q̂k=+∞\hat q_k=+\infty also when the rkr_k-th calibration score of stratum kk is +∞+\infty, and the reported set is then Bk∩DB_k\cap D rather than BkB_k. Second, the upper bound of Theorem 1 requires P(Y∉D)=0P(Y\notin D)=0. We report the fraction of test targets outside DD and how often q̂k=+∞\hat q_k=+\infty occurs.

Set geometry. Only the size, the number of pieces, the hull and the tail alerts of a set are computed numerically. For a test point, Ĉ(x)∩Bk={μ̂(x)+σ̂(x)u:ĝ(u)≥−q̂kσ̂(x)}∩Bk\hat C(x)\cap B_k=\{\hat\mu(x)+\hat\sigma(x)u:\hat g(u)\ge-\hat q_k\hat\sigma(x)\}\cap B_k. We tabulate ĝ\hat g on a non-uniform standardised grid (dense over the bulk of the residuals, logarithmically spaced beyond, analytic tt tails outside), interpolate linearly within each cell, and split every cell exactly at the stratum boundaries and the bounds of DD. The reported geometry is therefore that of the stratum-exact set for the piecewise-linear interpolant of ĝ\hat g. A grid-convergence check on six large or heavy-tailed datasets (Supplementary Section S3, Table S4) shows that a four times finer grid changes mean set sizes by at most 0.2% and individual set sizes by at most 1.5%. The same construction is used for every location–scale baseline (DLS, DCP, HPD-split, S-HPD, SDLC-N). Interval methods report half-open stratum pieces, so that a candidate on a boundary belongs to exactly one stratum, as in (4).

Algorithm 1 (SDLC). Input: 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}, 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}, levels αk\alpha_k, strata probabilities. (i) On 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}: fit μ̂\hat\mu; compute three-fold out-of-fold residuals; fit σ̃\tilde\sigma on all absolute out-of-fold residuals and three cross-fitted scale models; fit ĝ\hat g by (9) to the cross-fitted standardised residuals; build the strata from training targets. (ii) For each calibration point compute Si=−f̂(Yi|Xi)S_i=-\hat f(Y_i\,|\, X_i) (or +∞+\infty outside DD) and its stratum k(Yi)k(Y_i). (iii) Compute q̂k\hat q_k by (3) within each stratum. (iv) For a test xx, return {y∈D:f̂(y|x)≥−q̂k(y)}\{y\in D:\hat f(y\,|\, x)\ge-\hat q_{k(y)}\}. Cost: fitting requires eight gradient-boosted regressions (one mean model, three out-of-fold mean models, one full-data and three cross-fitted scale models); the kernel estimate costs O(N+GglogGg)O(N+G_g\log G_g) by linear binning and FFT convolution on GgG_g grid points. Calibration is O(nlogn)O(n\log n). Prediction costs O(GlogK)O(G\log K) per test point for a grid of GG standardised points, and one fit serves every α\alpha.

4.5 Two practical variants

Hull variant (SDLC-hull). When an interval is required, the convex hull of Ĉ(x)\hat C(x) is reported. It contains Ĉ(x)\hat C(x) and therefore inherits (5); the upper bound of Theorem 1 and the optimality of Proposition 2 do not carry over, and when some q̂k=+∞\hat q_k=+\infty the hull spans most of DD.

Floor variant (SDLC-floor). A user may want the efficiency of a single marginal threshold while protecting rare strata at a lower level 1−β1-\beta. The set Ĉfloor(x)={y:s(x,y)≤max(q̂αmarg,q̂k(y)(β))}\hat C_{\mathrm{floor}}(x)=\{y: s(x,y)\le\max(\hat q^{\mathrm{marg}}_\alpha,\hat q_{k(y)}(\beta))\}, with q̂αmarg\hat q^{\mathrm{marg}}_\alpha the ordinary split-conformal quantile at level α\alpha and q̂k(β)\hat q_k(\beta) the stratified quantile (3) at level β\beta, contains both the marginal set and the stratified set at level β\beta. It therefore has marginal coverage ≥1−α\ge 1-\alpha and stratum-wise coverage ≥1−β\ge 1-\beta simultaneously, in finite samples and for any β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1); we use β=2α\beta=2\alpha. This is a simple and conservative rule, not a contribution of the paper. Level-optimising schemes that trade coverage between bins (Wang et al., 2023) or choose group-specific levels to minimise length (Kiyani et al., 2024) are principled alternatives.

5. Experimental design

The study answers six research questions (RQs), each tied to one experiment. The datasets, seeds, splits, miscoverage levels, strata, base learners, method list and analyses of the main benchmark were fixed in a version-controlled configuration before the benchmark was run; Section 5.7 states what was and what was not fixed in advance.

  • RQ1 (tail coverage). Do marginal and covariate-adaptive conformal methods under-cover rare target strata on real data, and does stratified calibration restore stratum-wise coverage? Experiment 1: main benchmark.
  • RQ2 (price). How much larger are the sets when stratum-wise validity is required, compared with marginal methods at the same and at a stricter miscoverage level? Experiment 2: paired comparison of each score under marginal and stratified calibration.
  • RQ3 (score). Does the density-level score of Proposition 2 give smaller stratified sets than residual, normalised-residual, quantile and HPD scores, and which component of the score is responsible? Experiment 3: score ablation and decomposition on real data, a synthetic study with known densities, and a confirmatory replication on held-out datasets.
  • RQ4 (shift). How robust is stratum-wise coverage when the target distribution shifts? Experiment 4: a positive-control shift that re-weights whole strata (Corollary 1(i) applies), continuous tilts that also re-weight within strata (it does not), and a genuine label shift in the synthetic study.
  • RQ5 (decisions). Are prediction sets useful for flagging extreme outcomes, compared with dedicated conformal tail classifiers and conformal selection? Experiment 5: tail-alert decision study with expected-cost analysis.
  • RQ6 (robustness). How sensitive are the conclusions to the miscoverage level, the strata, the calibration-set size, the density estimator, the base learner and imbalance-aware training? Experiment 6: sensitivity analyses. Computational cost and an error analysis complete the evaluation.

5.1 Datasets

The main benchmark uses the OpenML-CTR23 suite, a curated benchmark of 35 tabular regression datasets with 500–100,000 observations and documented provenance (Fischer et al., 2023). Using a complete, externally curated suite avoids selecting datasets that favour the proposed method. We excluded, by a rule fixed in advance, the four datasets whose target takes fewer than 20 distinct values (red and white wine quality, solar flares, student performance), because for ordinal targets with a handful of values Lebesgue set size does not measure informativeness. The rule does not remove targets with many distinct values but heavy ties or atoms: weekly working hours (health insurance) and the burned area of forest fires, which is zero for 47.8% of the fires, are retained and analysed separately because their realised strata depart from the nominal ones. The remaining 31 datasets (Supplementary Table S1) range from 517 to 72,000 observations and from 5 to 971 features after one-hot encoding; 15 have a target skewness above 1 in absolute value. Categorical features were one-hot encoded and missing values were passed to the gradient-boosting models, which handle them natively.

Confirmatory datasets. For the replication (Experiment 3), we assembled before any confirmatory computation the regression datasets of the tabular benchmark of Grinsztajn et al. (2022) (OpenML suites 335 and 336). We removed every dataset that shares source data with a CTR23 dataset (for example house sales, Miami housing, superconductivity and diamonds) and duplicate versions, and applied the same exclusion rule. This left 17 held-out datasets with up to 50,000 observations (larger datasets were subsampled once, with a fixed seed); they are listed in Supplementary Table S2.

5.2 Splitting, leakage control and repetitions

Each of the 10 predefined seeds (0–9) defines a random partition into proper training (50%), calibration (25%) and test (25%) sets; the replication uses seeds 0–4. Every model, every stratum boundary and every density estimate uses the proper training set only; early stopping uses a 10% internal validation split of the proper training set, and calibration and test data are never used for fitting. Random splitting makes the rows of a dataset exchangeable, which is all that Theorem 1 requires, but several datasets contain repeated units: exact duplicate rows (for example 9.1% of sarcos, whose test set was appended to its training set), many transcodings of the same video (video transcoding), repeat sales (King County) and team-season panels (Moneyball). The guarantees therefore refer to a new row drawn from the same pool, not to a new video, a new house or a future season; Supplementary Section S2 reports the leakage audit (Table S3). Three small datasets (airfoil, concrete, QSAR fish toxicity) were used during development to choose the density estimator, and seven further datasets were used to diagnose the implementation (Section 5.7); the main comparisons are repeated without these ten datasets.

5.3 Base learners

All methods share the same LightGBM models (Ke et al., 2017) with a single fixed configuration (learning rate 0.05, 31 leaves, minimum 20 samples per leaf, row and column subsampling 0.8, ℓ2\ell_2 penalty 1, up to 2000 rounds with early stopping after 50 rounds): a mean model μ̂\hat\mu, quantile models at α/2\alpha/2 and 1−α/21-\alpha/2 (for CQR), the scale models of Algorithm 1, and a multiclass model over 40 equal-mass target bins (histogram density). No method receives method-specific tuning, so differences between methods reflect the conformal procedures and not the base learners. Two further learner settings are used in Experiment 6: a two-layer perceptron with the same pipeline (median imputation with missingness indicators, cross-fitted scales and the same floor), and LightGBM trained with DenseWeight sample weights, which up-weight rare targets (Steininger et al., 2021).

5.4 Compared methods

Marginal or covariate-adaptive calibration (baselines). Split conformal prediction with absolute residuals (SCP) (Lei et al., 2018; Papadopoulos et al., 2002); normalised (locally weighted) conformal prediction (NCP) (Lei et al., 2018); conformalised quantile regression (CQR) (Romano et al., 2019); Mondrian conformal regression with five equal-mass bins of the point prediction (Mondrian-ŷ), in the spirit of Boström and Johansson (2020) and Boruah (2026a); distributional conformal prediction (DCP) (Chernozhukov et al., 2021); HPD-split (Izbicki et al., 2022); and density level sets with a single threshold on the conditional density (DLS) (Izbicki et al., 2020; cf. Lei et al., 2013). DCP, HPD-split and DLS use the same location–scale density as SDLC, so the comparison with SDLC isolates the calibration rule.

Stratified calibration. BCCP (Randahl et al., 2026), i.e. the absolute-residual score with stratum-wise thresholds, in its union form and its hull (“contiguized”) form (BCCP-hull); the normalised-residual score with stratum-wise thresholds (S-NCP), in union and hull form; stratified CQR (S-CQR), the CQR score with stratum-wise thresholds; the HPD score with stratum-wise thresholds (S-HPD); and the proposed SDLC with its hull and floor (β=2α\beta=2\alpha) variants. S-CQR is related to the binned calibration of Wang et al. (2023) but omits its level optimisation and uses strata from training quantiles, so it should not be read as an implementation of BFQR. S-NCP is the information-matched comparator of SDLC: both use the same μ̂\hat\mu and σ̂\hat\sigma, and SDLC adds the noise density.

Ablations of the score. SDLC-N replaces the kernel estimate ĝ\hat g by a Gaussian density, so that the chain BCCP → S-NCP → SDLC-N → SDLC adds, in turn, the scale σ̂(x)\hat\sigma(x), the density weighting 1/σ̂(x)1/\hat\sigma(x), and the estimated noise shape. Two alternative densities are reported as secondary results: the multiclass histogram density and an exploratory two-piece location–scale density.

Dedicated tail-alert rules (Experiment 5). A set raises an upper-tail alert when it intersects the upper stratum (outcomes above the training 90% quantile); for every method with stratum-wise coverage 1−α1-\alpha the alert recall is at least 1−α1-\alpha. We compare such alerts with three rules built from the same models: a class-conditional conformal tail classifier (TC-LS), which thresholds the probability P̂(Y∈BK|x)\hat P(Y\in B_K\,|\, x) of the location–scale model so that the recall is at least 1−α1-\alpha; the same classifier with the probability from the histogram model (TC-H); and conformal selection with Benjamini–Hochberg control of the false discovery rate at q∈{0.1,0.2}q\in\{0.1,0.2\} (Jin and Candès, 2023). The naive rule “alert if μ̂(x)\hat\mu(x) is in the tail” is included as a reference without guarantee.

Implementation. All methods are fitted once per dataset and seed. Model outputs are cached, and every method is evaluated from the same cached outputs with the exact rules of Section 4.4.

5.5 Evaluation metrics

For each test set we report:

  • marginal coverage, and stratum-wise coverage (1) in each of the KK calibration strata;
  • coverage in strata not used for calibration: the training-target deciles, the top and bottom 5% and 1%, and the deciles of σ̂(x)\hat\sigma(x), the last as a diagnostic of covariate-conditional coverage together with worst-slab coverage (WSC) (Cauchois et al., 2021);
  • mean set size divided by the training-target standard deviation (normalised size), the share of empty sets and the mean number of disjoint pieces per set;
  • tail-alert recall, alert rate and precision, and the expected cost per unit when a missed extreme outcome costs rr times a false alert;
  • coverage under shift, computed by importance weighting of the test set: tilts w(y)=exp(γzy)w(y)=\exp(\gamma z_y) towards the upper tail (γ∈{1,2}\gamma\in\{1,2\}), the lower tail and both tails, where zyz_y is the normal score of yy under the training distribution, and a positive control that multiplies the upper stratum by 5 and the lower stratum by 0.5 without changing the within-stratum laws, so that Corollary 1(i) applies exactly. We report the Kish effective sample size of the weights and repeat the shift analysis on the datasets where it is at least 50.

Stratum coverages are averaged over seeds before taking the minimum across strata (“worst-stratum coverage”). This reduces, but does not remove, the downward bias of a minimum over noisy estimates (cf. Boruah, 2026b). We therefore also report a null reference: the worst-stratum coverage expected under exact conformal validity, given the realised calibration and test stratum sizes (Monte Carlo over the Beta–binomial law of split-conformal coverage). Computing time is recorded for every fit and for calibration plus prediction.

5.6 Statistical analysis

Following Demšar (2006), the unit of analysis is the dataset: metrics are averaged over seeds within each dataset and methods are compared across datasets. Set sizes are compared on the log scale and summarised by the geometric-mean ratio with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval (10,000 resamples of datasets), together with the Hodges–Lehmann estimate and its Wilcoxon-inversion confidence interval, the numbers of wins and losses, and the sign test. Paired comparisons use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Holm’s step-down correction within each family (Holm, 1979), and the matched-pairs rank-biserial correlation as effect size. One-sided alternatives are used only for the directional hypothesis that stratified calibration improves worst-stratum and tail coverage over marginal methods; all comparisons among stratified methods are two-sided. Equivalence of worst-stratum coverage between stratified methods is assessed by two one-sided Wilcoxon tests (TOST) with a margin of 0.01. Friedman mean ranks are reported descriptively only, because mean-rank post-hoc comparisons depend on which other methods are included (Benavoli et al., 2016).

5.7 Protocol, deviations and confirmatory replication

What was fixed in advance. The configuration of the main benchmark (datasets, exclusion rule, seeds, split proportions, miscoverage levels α∈{0.05,0.1,0.2}\alpha\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2\}, strata, base learners, the original method list and the sensitivity analyses), the primary method (SDLC with the location–scale density) and directional expectations for RQ1–RQ6 were committed to version control before the benchmark was run. These expectations were not registered with a third party, and we do not call the study pre-registered.

What changed afterwards. (1) An audit found that string-typed features had been parsed as missing values (month and day in the forest-fire data); the loader was corrected and every dataset with string-typed features was re-processed and recomputed. (2) After the first run we learned of BCCP and BFQR; BCCP’s hull form, the decile-stratified variants and tail-alert metrics were added. (3) The first implementation evaluated all density-based sets on a fixed grid of 200 equal-mass cells of the marginal target distribution, which inflates sets whenever the conditional density is narrower than a cell, for baselines and proposed method alike. Under that implementation the size comparison with BCCP was not significant (Supplementary Section S5). (4) A review of the second run identified further weaknesses that we corrected for every method: the noise density was fitted to residuals standardised by an in-sample scale model (now cross-fitted), the density had an ad hoc floor (now a defensive tt component), interval methods used closed stratum pieces (now half-open), the domain included impossible negative values (now truncated), and the set geometry was computed on a per-xx grid (now stratum-exact). All reported results use the final implementation; earlier results are archived with the code.

Consequences. Because the implementation changed after results had been seen, every size comparison on CTR23 (RQ3) is treated as exploratory. The coverage results (RQ1, RQ2, RQ4) are unaffected in direction by any of these changes. To test the size comparisons, we fixed a confirmatory analysis plan (hypotheses, tests, decision rules and analysis script; Supplementary Section S6) and committed it to the public repository before evaluating any method on the 17 held-out datasets. Section 6.5 reports the outcome whatever its direction.

6. Results

All results refer to α=0.1\alpha=0.1 and the primary five-stratum design unless stated otherwise. Each of the 31 datasets contributes the mean over its 10 splits (310 runs in total), and set sizes are normalised by the standard deviation of the training targets. 6.1 Marginal and covariate-adaptive methods under-cover the tails (RQ1)

All methods attained their nominal marginal coverage. Coverage of the target strata, however, differed sharply. The seven marginal or covariate-adaptive methods covered 69.0%–82.0% of the upper-tail targets and 44.5%–65.5% of the top 1%, and their worst-stratum coverage was 63.0%–78.3%. On 26–31 of the 31 datasets, it was below the range expected under exact validity. Fig. 1 shows the pattern: marginal methods over-cover the central deciles and pay for it in the outer ones, as Section 3 predicts. Covariate adaptivity reduces the shortfall (NCP, DCP and HPD-split are better than SCP and CQR) but does not remove it. Every stratified method, in contrast, covered 90.6%–90.9% of the upper tail, with worst-stratum coverage 89.0%–89.3%, and was below the null range on at most 2 datasets, as expected under exact validity. SDLC’s worst-stratum coverage exceeded that of each marginal method on at least 29 of 31 datasets (one-sided Holm-adjusted p≤p\le < 0.001; Hodges–Lehmann differences 0.081–0.250). The result is unchanged without the development datasets (p≤p\le < 0.001) and for upper-tail coverage alone (p≤p\le < 0.001). Protection extends partly beyond the calibrated strata: SDLC covered 86.8% of the top 5% and 73.6% of the top 1%, against at most 77.0% and 65.5% for the marginal methods. The top 1% is not calibrated, however, and its coverage remains below the nominal level for every method.

6.2 The price of stratum-wise validity (RQ2)

Stratum-wise validity enlarges the sets (Table 3). Holding the score fixed, stratified calibration increased the geometric-mean size by factors of 1.17 (normalised residual) to 1.27 (absolute residual). For SDLC relative to the single-threshold density level set (DLS) the factor was 1.24 (1.12–1.45), with a median of 1.11, for a gain in worst-stratum coverage of 0.231 (between 0.126 and 0.260 across scores). The price was concentrated: it exceeded 1.5 on only 3 datasets for SDLC (Section 6.9).

A fairer view of the price compares stratified sets with marginal sets that buy tail coverage by lowering α\alpha (Table 4). At α=0.05\alpha=0.05 every marginal method still had a lower worst-stratum coverage (0.772–0.878) than SDLC at α=0.1\alpha=0.1 (0.891), and SDLC’s sets were smaller than theirs on 23–28 of the 31 datasets. Raising the overall coverage level is therefore an inefficient way to protect the tails: calibrating within strata gives more tail coverage for less size.

6.3 The density score gives the smallest stratum-valid sets (RQ3)

Among the stratified methods, which all had equivalent worst-stratum coverage (TOST with margin 0.01: p≤p\le < 0.001 for every comparison with SDLC), SDLC produced the smallest sets (Table 5, Fig. 2). Its sets were smaller than those of BCCP on 24 of 31 datasets (geometric-mean ratio 0.902, 95% CI 0.841–0.956; Holm-adjusted pp < 0.001), than those of stratified CQR on 27 (ratio 0.795) and than those of S-HPD on 28 (ratio 0.947). Against the information-matched S-NCP, which uses the same μ̂\hat\mu and σ̂\hat\sigma, SDLC was smaller on 27 datasets (Holm pp < 0.001; Hodges–Lehmann ratio 0.962), but the gain was small and its geometric-mean ratio, 0.975 (0.941–1.020), was pulled towards one by a few datasets with large losses (Section 6.9). When an interval is required, SDLC-hull was smaller than BCCP-hull (ratio 0.903, 25/6), whereas against S-NCP-hull the median favoured SDLC-hull (23/8, Hodges–Lehmann ratio 0.979) and the geometric mean did not (1.014). Because the implementation of the density-based methods was changed after earlier results had been seen (Section 5.7), we treat these comparisons as exploratory; Section 6.5 tests them on held-out data.

The advantage was robust to the design choices (Supplementary Table S5). SDLC remained smaller than all four stratified comparators without the ten development and diagnostic datasets, on the 26 datasets whose realised tail strata are close to nominal, at α=0.05\alpha=0.05 and α=0.2\alpha=0.2, and with three or ten strata (Holm p≤p\le 0.002 in each of these analyses). Two subsets were less clear. On the 9 datasets with fewer than 1,600 observations no stratified score was consistently better (SDLC vs S-NCP: 5/4). On the 15 strongly skewed datasets (||skewness|>1|>1), SDLC was smaller than BCCP and S-HPD, while its advantage over S-NCP (12/3, Holm pp = 0.127) and S-CQR (pp = 0.127) was not significant.

Where the gain comes from. The ablation chain in Table 5 and Fig. 3 attributes the gain. Adding the scale σ̂(x)\hat\sigma(x) to the residual score (BCCP → S-NCP) reduced size on average (ratio 0.926) but not consistently (18/13 datasets, pp = 0.111). Replacing the normalised residual by a Gaussian density score, which only adds the factor 1/σ̂(x)1/\hat\sigma(x) (S-NCP → SDLC-N), reduced size on 26 of 31 datasets (pp < 0.001). Estimating the noise shape by the kernel density (SDLC-N → SDLC) added a further, smaller and less consistent reduction (ratio 0.993, 23/8, pp = 0.068). The two-piece density did not improve on the symmetric one (0.881 vs 0.874), and the histogram density, whose resolution is limited by its 40 bins, was far less efficient (1.745). The size advantage of SDLC over S-NCP is therefore mostly the coverage reallocation described in Section 4: the density score widens the sets of low-noise inputs and narrows those of high-noise inputs.

What the gain costs. The reallocation has a visible price, which the theory predicts and which a user should weigh. The worst coverage over deciles of σ̂(x)\hat\sigma(x) was 0.769 for SDLC against 0.793 for S-NCP (Fig. 4). SDLC returned empty sets for 0.36% of test points (S-NCP 0.07%), concentrated on the noisiest inputs of high-R2R^2 datasets. SDLC also covered fewer of the most extreme outcomes than S-NCP and S-HPD: 0.736 of the top 1% against 0.789 and 0.790 (Holm pp = 0.031 and 0.017). It covered more than BCCP and S-CQR, however (0.687 and 0.698). Within the calibrated strata these differences cancel, so that stratum-wise coverage is the same for all stratified methods.

6.4 Synthetic study with known densities

The synthetic study separates the score from its estimate (Table 6). It covers five designs with 5,000 training and calibration points each: skewed location–scale noise (A), covariate-dependent skewness (B), covariate-dependent bimodality (C), heavy tails (D) and a zero-inflated outcome without a density (E). With the true density, the oracle SDLC set was smaller than the oracle normalised residual in every design. The gain ranged from 2.9% to 35.2%, and the largest gain occurred for the bimodal design C, where the density level set excludes the gap between the modes. The estimated SDLC was smaller than S-NCP in 41 of the 50 design-seed combinations and smaller than BCCP in 50. Its sets were nevertheless much larger than the oracle’s when the location–scale model was misspecified: for design C they were 53.2% larger than the oracle SDLC set. The exactly covariate-conditional oracle (O-HDR-X) covered only 0.693 of the upper stratum in design A but 0.897 in the bimodal design C, which illustrates that the size of the shortfall depends on the model (Section 3). With only 500 training and calibration points, SDLC was smaller than S-NCP in 15 of 20 combinations, with smaller gains. Under a genuine label shift, in which X|YX\,|\, Y is unchanged (Supplementary Table S10), all stratified methods degraded similarly as the shift moved mass within the upper stratum. At γ=1\gamma=1 in design A they covered 0.811–0.824 of the upper stratum, close to the oracle SDLC (0.825), while the marginal methods fell to 0.581–0.607.

6.5 Confirmatory replication on held-out datasets

On the 17 held-out datasets, analysed exactly as pre-registered (Supplementary Section S6), all four hypotheses were supported (Table 7).

  • C-H1 (tail coverage). SDLC’s worst-stratum coverage exceeded that of each of the seven marginal and covariate-adaptive methods (Holm pp < 0.001).
  • C-H2 (validity). Its worst-stratum coverage fell below the 5% quantile of the exact-validity null reference on 1 of 17 datasets (critical value 3).
  • C-H3 (set size). SDLC’s sets were smaller than those of BCCP (geometric-mean ratio 0.862, 14/3 datasets, Holm pp = 0.001), S-CQR (0.841, 15/2, pp < 0.001), S-NCP (0.977, 15/2, pp = 0.008) and S-HPD (0.984, 15/2, pp = 0.008). By the pre-registered rule, every comparison favours SDLC. The gains over S-NCP and S-HPD are again small and consistent: the bootstrap intervals of their geometric-mean ratios (0.940–1.028 and 0.963–1.014) include one, while the signed-rank and sign tests show that the reduction occurs on most datasets.
  • C-H4 (equivalence). The worst-stratum coverage of SDLC was equivalent to that of S-NCP and BCCP within 0.02 (TOST pp < 0.001 and < 0.001).

The secondary results repeated the trade-off seen on CTR23. SDLC covered 0.747 of the top 1%, against 0.781 for S-NCP, and its worst coverage over deciles of σ̂(x)\hat\sigma(x) was 0.817, against 0.831. The price of stratification relative to DLS was 1.22, close to that on CTR23.

6.6 Target shift (RQ4)

Table 8 and Fig. 5 report coverage under shift. Under the positive control, which re-weights whole strata, the stratum-wise coverage of every stratified method was unchanged, as Corollary 1(i) states. Their marginal coverage stayed at the nominal level (0.904 for SDLC), whereas that of the marginal methods fell to 0.838–0.877. Continuous tilts towards the upper tail also re-weight targets within strata, so Corollary 1(i) does not apply. Under a moderate tilt (γ=1\gamma=1) the stratified methods kept 0.861–0.881 coverage of the upper stratum, against 0.633–0.783 for the marginal methods. Under a strong tilt (γ=2\gamma=2) every method lost coverage. The stratified methods lost less (0.770–0.833, against 0.550–0.726). Among them, SDLC (0.798) was below S-NCP and S-HPD (0.833), which is the same reallocation away from the most extreme outcomes seen above. The effective sample size of the γ=2\gamma=2 weights was small (median 49, minimum 5.9). Restricting the analysis to the 15 datasets with an effective sample size of at least 50 left the ordering unchanged. The bounds of Corollary 1(ii)–(iii) are not informative for these unbounded tilts. The synthetic study (Section 6.4) adds a genuine label shift with known X|YX\,|\, Y.

6.7 Tail alerts and decisions (RQ5)

A set that intersects the upper stratum raises an alert. Every stratified method guarantees an alert recall of at least 0.9; their mean recall was 0.978–0.988, and it was at least 0.9 on all 31 datasets (Table 9). The price of this conservativeness is a high alert rate. Among the stratified methods SDLC raised fewer alerts than BCCP (25/5 datasets) and S-CQR, but more than S-NCP (12/18). A dedicated conformal tail classifier built from the same location–scale model (TC-LS) attains the guaranteed recall almost exactly (mean 0.906) and raised fewer alerts than SDLC on every dataset (SDLC/TC-LS alert-rate ratio 1.559, SDLC lower on 0 of 31 datasets). For a pure yes/no decision about extremes, a dedicated classifier is therefore the more efficient tool. Conformal selection (Jin and Candès, 2023) controls the false discovery rate instead and flagged few units, with high precision (mean 0.766 at q=0.2q=0.2) but a mean recall of only 0.603; the naive point-prediction rule behaved similarly (recall 0.625).

Which rule is preferable depends on the cost of a missed extreme outcome relative to a false alert (Table 9). With equal costs, the rules that raise few alerts were cheapest: the point rule and conformal selection (expected cost 0.056 and 0.062 per unit, against 0.277 for SDLC). When a miss costs ten times a false alert, SDLC’s expected cost did not differ significantly from that of TC-LS (SDLC lower on 14 of 31 datasets, pp = 0.130) and was lower than that of conformal selection and of the point rule on 19 and 25 datasets. At a cost ratio of 20, SDLC was cheaper than TC-LS on 22 datasets (pp = 0.083), because its recall exceeds the guaranteed 0.9 while TC-LS attains it almost exactly. Alerts read off marginal sets (SCP, CQR, HPD-split) were the cheapest on average at high cost ratios (0.279 for HPD-split at r=20r=20). They had no recall guarantee, however, and their recall fell below 0.9 on 4–6 datasets. Fig. 6 shows the cost curves for three valuation problems (house prices in King County and Miami, wages in the CPS). The guarantee-free point rule and conformal selection become the most expensive rules as the cost ratio grows, and set-based alerts with stratum-wise coverage are the cheapest at the highest ratios. A set also carries more information than an alert: it says how large the outcome may be, which a downstream decision such as a provision, an inspection priority or a price range can use.
