6.8 Sensitivity analyses (RQ6)

Miscoverage level and strata. The conclusions held at α=0.05\alpha=0.05 and α=0.2\alpha=0.2 (Supplementary Table S6): stratified methods restored worst-stratum coverage to 0.947 and 0.789, and SDLC had the smallest stratified sets. Finer strata protected narrower ranges of the target: with decile strata (S10) the worst decile coverage of SDLC rose to 0.888, from 0.863 with five strata, at a size increase from 0.874 to 0.898. The floor variant (SDLC-floor, β=0.2\beta=0.2) reached its weaker guarantee with smaller sets (worst stratum 0.821, size 0.806).

Calibration-set size. Stratified calibration needs enough calibration points in every stratum (Supplementary Fig. S3, Table S8). With a quarter of the calibration split (on average 1,082 points) stratum-wise validity was retained, but the stratified sets grew from 0.874 to 1.243 for SDLC. The main reason was that a tail stratum with fewer than 1/α−11/\alpha-1 points has an infinite threshold, which happened in 87 runs, against 2 with the full split. Marginal methods are insensitive to this, and for small datasets stratified calibration should be combined with fewer strata or a lower stratum level β\beta (the floor variant).

Density estimator. Among the density estimators, the symmetric location–scale density was as efficient as the two-piece variant and much more efficient than the histogram density (Table 5); the defensive tt component and the cross-fitted standardisation are part of every result reported here.

Base learner. With a two-layer perceptron as point and scale model (same pipeline, 5 seeds), the coverage results were unchanged: marginal methods reached a worst-stratum coverage of 0.650–0.830, stratified methods 0.889–0.891. SDLC again gave the smallest stratified sets: smaller than BCCP on 23 of 31 datasets (ratio 0.946, Holm pp = 0.019), than S-NCP on 27 (ratio 0.938, pp < 0.001) and than S-HPD on 29 (ratio 0.927, pp < 0.001). The gain over S-NCP was larger than with gradient boosting.

Imbalance-aware training. Does a base learner trained for imbalanced regression remove the need for stratified calibration? With DenseWeight sample weights (Steininger et al., 2021) (seeds 0–2), the marginal methods covered the tails better than with unweighted training on the same splits: SCP’s worst-stratum coverage rose from 0.630 to 0.759, and CQR’s from 0.720 to 0.775. The shortfall remained large, however, and the sets grew by factors of 1.31 (SCP) and 1.45 (CQR). Stratified calibration remained valid with the weighted learner (0.885 for SDLC), and SDLC again gave the smallest stratified sets (ratios 0.906, 0.948, 0.694 and 0.964 against BCCP, S-NCP, S-CQR and S-HPD; Holm pp < 0.001 or smaller). Imbalance-aware point learning and stratified calibration are thus complementary, and the former does not deliver the coverage guarantee.

Repeated units. Three datasets contain repeated units that a random split separates: exact duplicate rows in sarcos, several encodings of the same input video in video transcoding, and identical feature vectors in superconductivity. We re-ran the pipeline with splits that keep each unit in one part (sarcos deduplicated; seeds 0–4; Supplementary Table S14). For sarcos and superconductivity the results were practically unchanged: stratified methods kept a worst-stratum coverage of at least 0.889 and 0.879, and SDLC remained smaller than S-NCP (ratios 0.97 and 0.91) and BCCP (0.89 and 0.82). Video transcoding behaved differently. With grouped splits the point and scale models no longer see other encodings of a test video, and all sets became much longer (SDLC 0.113 → 0.775 sd(yy)): the small random-split sets owe much to the repeated units. Marginal methods lost more tail coverage than under random splits (worst stratum at most 0.766), while the worst stratum of the stratified methods stayed at 0.852 or above. Some stratified methods also fell below the nominal level overall (BCCP 0.875, S-CQR 0.873); the guarantee holds on average over splits, and with only about 1,100 units the coverage of a single split varies strongly, so five splits cannot separate this from a violation. SDLC was smaller than S-NCP (ratio 0.88) but larger than BCCP (1.20): when the location and scale models transfer poorly to new units, the density score, which relies on them, loses its advantage over the plain residual score of BCCP. Random splits therefore overstate the efficiency of all methods on data with repeated units, and SDLC’s size advantage over BCCP should not be assumed there.

Computation. On one CPU thread the exact SDLC sets took a median of 13.1 µs per test point over the 31 datasets (Supplementary Table S13; maximum over datasets 90.5 µs), the same order as the other exact density-based methods (HPD-split 13.1 µs, DLS 14.0 µs) and about two orders of magnitude slower than interval methods such as BCCP (0.06 µs); calibration adds one score per calibration point. The extra fitting cost of SDLC beyond the point and scale models — cross-fitted standardisation and the noise density — was 2.9 s and 0.004 s on the largest dataset (wave energy, 36,000 training points), against 63.3 s for the histogram classifier used by the histogram-density methods (Supplementary Table S15).

6.9 Error analysis

Where does stratification cost the most, and where does SDLC lose to simpler scores? The price of stratum-wise validity (SDLC relative to DLS) rose with the skewness of the target (Spearman ρ\rho = 0.62, pp < 0.001) and fell with the calibration-set size (ρ\rho = -0.41, pp = 0.022); it was weakly related to the predictability of the target (ρ\rho = 0.38, pp = 0.034). The largest price occurred for forest fires (8.75): the burned area is zero for 47.8% of the fires, the atom at zero merges the two lower strata, and covering the heavy upper tail of an almost unpredictable target requires very long sets. SDLC was larger than S-NCP on 4 datasets: the social-mobility table (socmob, ratio 1.64), cars (1.20), forest fires (1.03) and QSAR fish toxicity (1.01). All four are small or have many ties, so that the scale and noise models are estimated from few distinct values. The ratio of SDLC to S-NCP was correlated with the relative RMSE of the point model (ρ\rho = 0.47, pp = 0.008): the density score helps most when the location model is accurate and the noise is heteroscedastic. Supplementary Fig. S2 relates the worst-stratum coverage of each dataset to its null reference; the lowest values occur on the smallest calibration sets and remain within the range expected under exact validity.

7. Discussion

7.1 What the evidence supports

Three findings are robust across datasets, miscoverage levels, stratifications and learner families. First, marginal and covariate-adaptive conformal methods systematically under-cover rare targets. Their worst-stratum coverage at a nominal 90% was 63.0%–78.3% on average, and the null reference shows that this is not sampling noise. The oracle analysis (Section 3) and the synthetic study show that the shortfall is not an artefact of estimation, although its size depends on the data-generating process. Second, calibrating within target strata restores stratum-wise coverage for every score, as Mondrian theory guarantees and as BCCP (Randahl et al., 2026) showed in simulations and one application. In our benchmark the guarantee held across 31 datasets, resisted moderate target shift, and cost a geometric-mean size increase of 1.17–1.27-fold. It is also the efficient way to protect the tails: lowering α\alpha for a marginal method bought less tail coverage at a larger size. Third, the score matters for efficiency in the direction predicted by Proposition 2. The density score gave smaller stratum-valid sets than the residual score of BCCP, the quantile score and the HPD score on most datasets, and the synthetic study confirms the ordering with known densities. The size ordering was confirmed on 17 held-out datasets under a pre-registered analysis plan.

Two qualifications are equally well supported. The gain of the density score over the information-matched normalised residual is small, a few per cent, and it comes mainly from the factor 1/σ̂(x)1/\hat\sigma(x), that is, from reallocating coverage from noisy to quiet inputs. Its price is lower coverage of the noisiest inputs, occasional empty sets and lower coverage of the most extreme 1% of outcomes, which is not calibrated. Moreover, the estimated location–scale density is far from the oracle when the noise shape changes with xx: in the bimodal synthetic design the oracle density set was much smaller than any estimated stratified set. The ranking of scores is therefore a statement about efficiency on average, not a free improvement.

7.2 Practical guidance

For practitioners who must report how often extreme outcomes are covered, the results suggest the following.

  1. Calibrate within strata whenever coverage of rare targets is a requirement. Marginal coverage, however adaptive the score, does not deliver it, and lowering α\alpha is a less efficient substitute.
  2. Choose strata from training-target quantiles so that each stratum receives at least several times 1/α1/\alpha calibration points; otherwise the method returns whole strata. Finer strata extend protection to narrower target ranges at a modest cost in size. With small calibration sets, use fewer strata or the floor variant.
  3. Choose the score by the secondary property that matters. SDLC gives the smallest stratum-valid sets on average. S-NCP is almost as small, simpler, and spreads coverage more evenly across noise levels and into the extreme 1%. BCCP and stratified CQR were the least efficient.
  4. Report hulls when an interval is mandatory. Stratified sets can be discontiguous: SDLC’s sets had 1.527 pieces on average (BCCP 1.465), mostly an isolated piece in a tail stratum whose threshold is lower than that of its neighbour (Fig. 7). Such a piece is informative, because it says that an extreme outcome is plausible, but an interval is easier to communicate. SDLC-hull is valid and remains smaller than BCCP-hull, but it loses part of the advantage.
  5. For yes/no decisions about extremes, match the rule to the costs. A class-conditional conformal tail classifier attains the same recall guarantee with fewer alerts and is the better choice when false alerts are expensive. Set-based alerts have higher recall, are cheaper when misses are very costly, and carry more information about the size of the outcome.

7.3 Limitations

Size cost and data requirements. Stratum-wise validity is paid for in set size, and the payment grows with skewness and when tail strata are small. With a quarter of the calibration set, sets became considerably larger, and with fewer than 1/αk−11/\alpha_k-1 calibration points the method returns the whole stratum. Pooling sparse strata, as in clustered conformal prediction (Ding et al., 2023), cross-fitted calibration (Barber et al., 2021a) and overlapping or weighted groups as in Kandinsky conformal prediction (Bairaktari et al., 2025) are natural remedies that we did not evaluate. Any pooling rule must be decided from training data only to preserve validity.

Granularity of the guarantee. The guarantee holds for the calibrated strata, not for arbitrary sub-ranges. Within a stratum, coverage is lower near its outer end, and shifts that move mass within a stratum reduce coverage (Table 8); Corollary 1 explains the direction of this effect, but its bounds are loose for open tail strata. The guarantee is also marginal over XX within each stratum, so it says nothing about a particular input, and the density score deliberately trades coverage across inputs.

Density estimation and baselines. The optimality of Proposition 2 is an oracle property, and Proposition 3 requires a uniformly consistent density estimate, which the location–scale model provides only when the noise shape does not depend on xx. Flexible conditional density estimators (mixture density networks, normalising flows, distributional boosting) may close the gap to the oracle. We did not run several covariate-adaptive methods that could be stratified in the same way, such as conditional histograms (Sesia and Romano, 2021), conditional calibration (Gibbs et al., 2025) or localised conformal prediction (Hore and Barber, 2025); Proposition 2 implies that none of them can beat the oracle density score, but their estimated versions may be competitive.

Evaluation scope. The benchmark covers tabular data with targets having at least 20 distinct values; ordinal, count and temporally dependent targets were excluded. Several datasets contain repeated units (duplicate rows in sarcos, repeated videos, repeat sales, team-season panels). Random splitting keeps the rows exchangeable, so the guarantees hold for new rows from the same pool, but not for new units or future periods. Splits that keep repeated units together (Section 6.8) left the conclusions unchanged on two of three such datasets; on video transcoding all sets grew several-fold and SDLC lost its size advantage over BCCP, so efficiency estimates from random splits are optimistic for data with repeated units. All results are for split calibration with a 50/25/25 split and one fixed configuration of the base learners, chosen without tuning to avoid favouring any method. The implementation of the density-based methods changed after earlier results had been seen (Section 5.7); this is why the size comparisons on CTR23 are labelled exploratory and were replicated on held-out data.

Applicability of the guarantee. Like all conformal guarantees, stratum-wise coverage requires exchangeability of calibration and test data. It holds on average over calibration sets and over the test points of a stratum, and it does not protect against shifts of the covariate distribution within strata.

8. Conclusion

Prediction intervals that are valid on average can fail exactly where imbalanced regression needs them: on the rare outcomes. Even the oracle interval with exact covariate-conditional coverage under-covers the tails of the target, and on 31 benchmark datasets marginal and covariate-adaptive conformal methods covered only 63.0%–78.3% of the outcomes in their worst-covered stratum at a nominal 90%. Calibrating thresholds within strata of the target, an established Mondrian device, restores coverage of rare outcomes in finite samples for any score, holds exactly under shifts that re-weight whole strata, and buys more tail coverage per unit of size than lowering the miscoverage level.

The score then determines efficiency. Conditional-density level sets with stratum-specific thresholds are the smallest stratum-valid sets for the oracle, and their plug-in conformal version is asymptotically optimal. The resulting method, SDLC, gave smaller stratum-valid sets than bin-conditional conformal prediction with residual scores and than stratified quantile and HPD scores on most CTR23 datasets, and the ordering was confirmed on 17 held-out datasets under a pre-registered analysis. Its advantage over a stratified normalised residual is small and comes mostly from reallocating coverage from noisy to quiet inputs, at the price of lower coverage of the noisiest inputs and of the most extreme outcomes. For yes/no decisions about extremes, dedicated conformal tail classifiers attain the same recall guarantee with fewer alerts, whereas set-based alerts are cheaper when missed extremes are very costly.

Future work should combine stratified calibration with flexible conditional density estimators, whose gap to the oracle was largest under covariate-dependent multimodality; with data-efficient calibration for sparse strata and overlapping groups; and with dependent data.

Data. They were downloaded programmatically through the OpenML API by the scripts in the code package; the OpenML identifier and licence of each dataset are listed in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2.

Code. Appendix A. Proofs

Proof of Theorem 1. Condition on 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}, which fixes the score ss and the strata. Let Ek={Yn+1∈Bk}E_k=\{Y_{n+1}\in B_k\} and J={i≤n+1:Yi∈Bk}J=\{i\le n+1: Y_i\in B_k\}, so that |J|=nk+1|J|=n_k+1 on EkE_k. Membership of a point in BkB_k is a function of that point alone, so any permutation of {1,…,n+1}\{1,\ldots,n+1\} that maps JJ onto itself leaves the event {J=j,n+1∈J}\{J=j,\ n+1\in J\} unchanged; by exchangeability, conditionally on J=j∋n+1J=j\ni n+1 and on the multiset {(Xi,Yi):i∈j}\{(X_i,Y_i):i\in j\}, the index n+1n+1 is uniformly distributed over jj. Let RR be the rank of Sn+1=s(Xn+1,Yn+1)S_{n+1}=s(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1}) among {Si}i∈J\{S_i\}_{i\in J}, with ties broken uniformly at random; conditionally as above, RR is uniform on {1,…,nk+1}\{1,\ldots,n_k+1\}. By (3)–(4), Yn+1∈Ĉ(Xn+1)Y_{n+1}\in\hat C(X_{n+1}) iff Sn+1≤q̂kS_{n+1}\le\hat q_k, which holds whenever R≤rk=⌈(nk+1)(1−αk)⌉R\le r_k=\lceil(n_k+1)(1-\alpha_k)\rceil (if rk>nkr_k>n_k, then q̂k=+∞\hat q_k=+\infty and coverage is one). Hence the conditional coverage is at least rk/(nk+1)≥1−αkr_k/(n_k+1)\ge 1-\alpha_k. Averaging over JJ and the multiset gives (5); since the argument conditions on JJ, the level αk\alpha_k may depend on nkn_k. If scores are almost surely distinct, coverage is exactly min{rk,nk+1}/(nk+1)<1−αk+1/(nk+1)\min\{r_k,n_k+1\}/(n_k+1)<1-\alpha_k+1/(n_k+1) given nkn_k. The marginal statement follows from the law of total probability, ∑kpk(1−αk)=1−∑kpkαk\sum_kp_k(1-\alpha_k)=1-\sum_kp_k\alpha_k. Finally, the conditioning on 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} allows any score and strata that are measurable functions of 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} alone. ▫\square

Proof of Corollary 1. Given 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} and 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}} the set A={(x,y):y∈Ĉ(x)}A=\{(x,y):y\in\hat C(x)\} is fixed. Because the test point is independent of the calibration data, Q{Y∈Ĉ(X)|Y∈Bk}=𝔼Qk(A)Q\{Y\in\hat C(X)\,|\, Y\in B_k\}=\mathbb{E}\,Q_k(A) and the left-hand side of (5) equals 𝔼Pk(A)\mathbb{E}\,P_k(A), where 𝔼\mathbb{E} averages over 𝒟cal∼Pn\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}\sim P^n (i.i.d. data are exchangeable, so (5) applies). (i) If Qk=PkQ_k=P_k the two expectations coincide, and the law of total probability gives the marginal statement. (ii) |Qk(A)−Pk(A)|≤dTV(Qk,Pk)|Q_k(A)-P_k(A)|\le d_{\operatorname{TV}}(Q_k,P_k) for every fixed AA; average and use (5). (iii) Under label shift the likelihood ratio of QkQ_k to PkP_k is λk(y)=w(y)/w‾k\lambda_k(y)=w(y)/\bar w_k with w‾k=πk/pk=𝔼Pkw(Y)≥mk\bar w_k=\pi_k/p_k=\mathbb{E}_{P_k}w(Y)\ge m_k. Hence Qk(Ac)=𝔼Pk{λk(Y)𝟏Ac(X,Y)}≤(Mk/w‾k)Pk(Ac)≤(Mk/mk)Pk(Ac)Q_k(A^c)=\mathbb{E}_{P_k}\{\lambda_k(Y)\mathbf{1}_{A^c}(X,Y)\}\le(M_k/\bar w_k)P_k(A^c)\le(M_k/m_k)P_k(A^c); averaging over 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}} and using (5) gives the multiplicative bound. For the total-variation bound, λk∈[a,b]\lambda_k\in[a,b] with a=mk/w‾k≤1≤b=Mk/w‾ka=m_k/\bar w_k\le1\le b=M_k/\bar w_k and 𝔼Pkλk=1\mathbb{E}_{P_k}\lambda_k=1; since dTV(Qk,Pk)=𝔼Pk(λk−1)+d_{\operatorname{TV}}(Q_k,P_k)=\mathbb{E}_{P_k}(\lambda_k-1)_+ and, by convexity, (λ−1)+≤(b−1)(λ−a)/(b−a)(\lambda-1)_+\le(b-1)(\lambda-a)/(b-a) on [a,b][a,b], we obtain dTV≤(b−1)(1−a)/(b−a)=(Mk−w‾k)(w‾k−mk)/{w‾k(Mk−mk)}d_{\operatorname{TV}}\le(b-1)(1-a)/(b-a)=(M_k-\bar w_k)(\bar w_k-m_k)/\{\bar w_k(M_k-m_k)\}. The right-hand side is maximised at w‾k=mkMk\bar w_k=\sqrt{m_kM_k}, where it equals (Mk−mk)/(Mk+mk)=tanh{log(Mk/mk)/4}(\sqrt{M_k}-\sqrt{m_k})/(\sqrt{M_k}+\sqrt{m_k})=\tanh\{\log(M_k/m_k)/4\}. ▫\square

Otherwise the integrand of Δk=∬(𝟏Ak⋆−𝟏Ak)(f(y|x)−tk)dyPX(dx)\Delta_k=\iint\left(\mathbf{1}_{A_k^\star}-\mathbf{1}_{A_k}\right)\left(f(y\,|\, x)-t_k\right)dy\,P_X(dx) is non-negative pointwise: on Ak⋆\AkA_k^\star\setminus A_k we have f≥tkf\ge t_k, and on Ak\Ak⋆A_k\setminus A_k^\star, where y∈Bky\in B_k, we have f<tkf<t_k. Hence Δk≥0\Delta_k\ge 0, i.e. tk(|Ak⋆|P−|Ak|P)≤pk{Covk(C⋆)−Covk(C)}≤0t_k(|A_k^\star|_P-|A_k|_P)\le p_k\{\operatorname{Cov}_k(C^\star)-\operatorname{Cov}_k(C)\}\le 0, and tk>0t_k>0 gives |Ak⋆|P≤|Ak|P|A_k^\star|_P\le|A_k|_P. Proof of Proposition 3. Condition on 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} (hence on f̂\hat f) and write Vi=f(Yi|Xi)V_i=f(Y_i\,|\, X_i), V̂i=f̂(Yi|Xi)\hat V_i=\hat f(Y_i\,|\, X_i), so that |V̂i−Vi|≤εN|\hat V_i-V_i|\le\varepsilon_N. Thresholds. By (3), −q̂k-\hat q_k is the (nk+1−rk)(n_k+1-r_k)-th smallest of {V̂i:i∈Ik}\{\hat V_i:i\in I_k\}, and (nk+1−rk)/nk→αk(n_k+1-r_k)/n_k\to\alpha_k because nk→∞n_k\to\infty almost surely (nk∼Bin(n,pk)n_k\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p_k) given 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}). Order statistics are 1-Lipschitz in the sup-norm, so −q̂k-\hat q_k differs by at most εN\varepsilon_N from the same order statistic of {Vi:i∈Ik}\{V_i:i\in I_k\}. The ViV_i, i∈Iki\in I_k, are i.i.d. from the law of f(Y|X)f(Y\,|\, X) given Y∈BkY\in B_k, independent of 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}, whose αk\alpha_k-quantile tkt_k is unique by assumption; hence that order statistic converges to tkt_k almost surely (Serfling, 1980, sec. 2.3), and δk:=|q̂k+tk|→0\delta_k:=|\hat q_k+t_k|\to0 in probability. Sets. Fix xx and y∈Bky\in B_k. If yy lies in exactly one of Ĉ(x)\hat C(x) and C⋆(x)C^\star(x), then f̂(y|x)+q̂k\hat f(y\,|\, x)+\hat q_k and f(y|x)−tkf(y\,|\, x)-t_k have opposite signs (one is ≥0\ge0, the other <0<0), while they differ by at most εN+δk\varepsilon_N+\delta_k; hence |f(y|x)−tk|≤η:=εN+maxkδk|f(y\,|\, x)-t_k|\le\eta:=\varepsilon_N+\max_k\delta_k. Therefore 𝔼X|Ĉ(X)△C⋆(X)|≤∑k=1Khk(η),hk(η)=𝔼|{y∈Bk:|f(y|X)−tk|≤η}|.\mathbb{E}_X|\hat C(X)\triangle C^\star(X)|\le\sum_{k=1}^K h_k(\eta),\qquad h_k(\eta)=\mathbb{E}\,\big|\{y\in B_k:|f(y\,|\, X)-t_k|\le\eta\}\big|. For η<tk/2\eta<t_k/2 the set inside hkh_k lies in {y:f(y|X)≥tk/2}\{y:f(y\,|\, X)\ge t_k/2\}, whose measure is at most 2/tk2/t_k, and it decreases to {y∈Bk:f(y|X)=tk}\{y\in B_k:f(y\,|\, X)=t_k\} as η↓0\eta\downarrow0. Since η→0\eta\to0 in probability, (7) follows, and ||Ĉ|−|C⋆||≤|Ĉ△C⋆||\,|\hat C|-|C^\star|\,|\le|\hat C\triangle C^\star| gives the statement on expected size. ▫\square

Remark (within-stratum coverage profile). Under label shift, let κ(y)=P{y∈Ĉ(Xn+1)|Yn+1=y}\kappa(y)=P\{y\in\hat C(X_{n+1})\,|\, Y_{n+1}=y\}, which is the same under PP and QQ. Then the change in stratum-wise coverage equals the within-stratum covariance 𝔼Pk[{κ(Y)−c}{λk(Y)−1}]\mathbb{E}_{P_k}[\{\kappa(Y)-c\}\{\lambda_k(Y)-1\}] for any constant cc, so coverage is lost only if the shift moves mass within BkB_k towards values that are covered less often than the stratum average. For the oracle sets C⋆C^\star in the Gaussian model of Proposition 1, C⋆(x)∩Bk={y∈Bk:|y−x|≤rk}C^\star(x)\cap B_k=\{y\in B_k:|y-x|\le r_k\} for a stratum-specific radius rkr_k, so the argument of Proposition 1 (with a=rka=r_k) shows that κ\kappa decreases in |y||y| within every stratum, that is, towards the outer end of a tail stratum; for the estimated sets the same pattern is observed empirically (Section 6). This is why a tilt towards more extreme outcomes can lower tail-stratum coverage even after stratified calibration.
